newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai firms seen delaying foreign bond issues.
newsitem.headline: Thai firms seen delaying foreign bond issues.

text.p: Jitters over Thailand's economy, its financial sector and the stability of the baht have forced some banks to delay raising funds abroad and more corporates are expected to put off debt issues, analysts said on Friday.
Market sentiment on Thai debt papers has been buffeted by negative news about the country, including uncertainty this week over government policy to revamp the foreign exchange regime.
"The timing is not right to issue these instruments. Do you realistically expect foreign investors to buy them with the situation Thailand faces now?" said a currency dealer at a Thai bank.

Siam Commercial Bank Plc said on Thursday it had put off its $150 million Yankee bond issue following the Bank of Thailand's decision to squeeze the supply of offshore baht after speculators attacked the currency in mid-May.

A Siam Commercial executive said the central bank measures, including a ban on the repatriation of baht funds by foreign stock investors, had eroded market confidence, which would translate into higher funding costs for the bank's bond issue.

The Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand late last week cancelled its plan to issue a $150 million, three-year floating rate note. The withdrawal followed downgrades of the institution's long and short-term counterparty ratings by Standard and Poor's Corp.

"The primary reason (for the shelving of the issues) rests with the central bank's lack of policy on the baht. Its shifting stand and policy leaves us confused about what's going on and what will happen next," said a foreign analyst who declined to be identified.
He said Thailand's tight control of baht supply complicated efforts by debt issuers to determine their funding costs and they would have to shoulder associated risk premiums.

Bangkok Bank Plc said on Friday it had not decided when to go ahead with its plans, approved by shareholders in March, to float $1.5 billion worth of subordinated perpetual bonds of 30-100 years and another $1.5 billion worth of 30-year debentures.

Bangkok Bank executive Piyapan Chayanithi said that under Thailand's sluggish economic conditions his bank had no immediate need to raise foreign funds, either for meeting its capital or domestic lending requirements.

"Major financial institutions could not avoid feeling the pinch of bad publicity generated by Finance One Plc and Bangkok Bank of Commerce Plc. You cannot quantify the cost of confidence crisis in term of basis points," a local currency dealer said.
Analysts said cash-strapped Finance One, Thailand's biggest finance firm, would likely need a government bailout after its merger talks with Thai Danu Bank Plc collapsed last month.
Bangkok Bank of Commerce, saddled with huge non- performing loans, was taken over by the government last year.

"Who would buy Thai debt papers? In the view of foreign investors, the recent debt defaults by Thai property firms should have some credibility impact on financial institutions here," the currency dealer said.

A fixed income fund manager said foreign investors in Thai debts had also been sidelined by a schedule for Thai banks and finance firms to disclose their non-performing and sub-standard assets next month.
